nodes.name: State (4.5) and split the integral
nodes.statement: We start by showing that \begin{equation} \lim_{k\to\infty} \intrn \frac{|v_{n_k}|^2}{|x|^2}dx = 0. \end{equation} To prove \eqref{zerolimit}, we split the integral as \[ \intrn \frac{|v_{n_k}|^2}{|x|^2}dx = \underbrace{\int_{|x|<R}\frac{|v_{n_k}|^2}{|x|^2}dx}_{\mathrm{I}_k} +\underbrace{\int_{|x|\ge R}\frac{|v_{n_k}|^2}{|x|^2}dx}_{\mathrm{II}_k}, \] for some $R>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Write $\int|v_{n_k}|^2/|x|^2=\mathrm I_k+\mathrm{II}_k$.

nodes.name: Outer part $\mathrm{II}_k$ is small
nodes.statement: We first observe that, by the boundedness of $\{v_{n_k}\}$ in $L^2(\rn)$, there exists $C\ge0$ such that \[ \mathrm{II}_k\le R^{-2}\int_{\rn}|v_{n_k}(x)|^2dx\le CR^{-2}. \] By choosing $R>0$ large, we can thus make $\mathrm{II}_k$ as small as we want, uniformly in $k$.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathrm{II}_k\le CR^{-2}$ uniformly in $k$.

nodes.name: Assume $\mathrm I_k\not\to0$
nodes.statement: Next, we fix $R>0$ arbitrary and prove that $\lim_{k\to\infty}\mathrm{I}_k=0$. This will complete the proof of \eqref{zerolimit}. We argue by contradiction and suppose there exist $\delta>0$ and a subsequence of $\{v_{n_k}\}$ (still denoted $\{v_{n_k}\}$) such that \begin{equation*} \liminf_{k\rightarrow\infty}\int_{|x|<R}\frac{|v_{n_k}|^2}{|x|^2}dx\ge\delta. \end{equation*} Note that this inequality will still hold if we increase the value of $R$ or pass to a further subsequence.
nodes.statement_short: Suppose $\liminf\int_{|x|<R}|v_{n_k}|^2/|x|^2\ge\delta>0$.

nodes.name: Cut-off decomposition $u_k$, $w_k$
nodes.statement:
Let $a>0$ and $ fi\in C_0^\infty([0,\infty))$ be such that $ fi(r)=1$ for $0\le r \le R$, $ fi(r)=0$ for $r\ge R+a$, $0\le fi\le1$ and $\| fi'\|_{L^\infty}\le 1/a$. Then define \[ u_k(x)= fi(|x|) v_{n_k}(x) \quad	ext{and}\quad w_k(x)=(1- fi(|x|))v_{n_k}(x). \] We clearly have $|u_k|,|w_k|\le|v_{n_k}|$, and $\{u_k\},\{w_k\}\subset H^1(n)$ with \[ |
abla u_k|^2 \le 2\left(( fi')^2|v_{n_k}|^2+ fi^2|
abla v_{n_k}|^2ight) \le 2\left(a^{-2}|v_{n_k}|^2+|
abla v_{n_k}|^2ight) \] and \[ |
abla w_k|^2 \le 2\left(( fi')^2|v_{n_k}|^2+(1- fi)^2|
abla v_{n_k}|^2ight) \le 2\left(a^{-2}|v_{n_k}|^2+|
abla v_{n_k}|^2ight). \]
nodes.statement_short: Define $u_k=\varphi v_{n_k}$, $w_k=(1-\varphi)v_{n_k}$ with gradient bounds.

nodes.name: Hardy lower bound (4.6) for $H(u_k)$
nodes.statement: Furthermore, \begin{equation*} \liminf_{k\rightarrow\infty}\intrn\frac{|u_k|^2}{|x|^2}dx\ge \liminf_{k\rightarrow\infty}\int_{|x|<R}\frac{|v_{n_k}|^2}{|x|^2}dx\ge\delta, \end{equation*} and \eqref{hardy} yields \begin{equation} \liminf_{k\rightarrow\infty}H(u_k)=\liminf_{k\rightarrow\infty} \left(\intrn |\nabla u_k|^2dx-c\intrn\frac{|u_k|^2}{|x|^2}dx\right) \ge (c_*-c)\delta>0. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Hardy's inequality gives $\liminf H(u_k)\ge(c_*-c)\delta>0$.

nodes.name: Decompose $H(v_{n_k})$
nodes.statement:
Using the sequences $\{u_k\},\{w_k\}$, we can now rewrite $H(v_{n_k})$ as  egin{align*} H(v_{n_k}) &=H(u_k)+H(w_k) \ &\phantom{=}+\int_{R<|x|<R+a} \Big[|
abla v_{n_k}|^2-|
abla u_k|^2-|
abla w_k|^2 - rac{c}{|x|^2}\left(|v_{n_k}|^2-|u_k|^2-|w_k|^2ight)\Big]dx. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: $H(v_{n_k})=H(u_k)+H(w_k)+$ an annulus interaction term.

nodes.name: Reduce to the annulus estimate (4.7)
nodes.statement:
We will show that there exist $R>0$ as large as we want and $a>0$ such that, up to a further subsequence,  egin{equation} \limsup_{k	o\infty}\left|\int_{R<|x|<R+a} \Big[|
abla v_{n_k}|^2-|
abla u_k|^2-|
abla w_k|^2 - rac{c}{|x|^2}\left(|v_{n_k}|^2-|u_k|^2-|w_k|^2ight)\Big]dxight|\le rac{(c_*-c)\delta}{2}. \end{equation} Using \eqref{crucial}, this will imply  egin{equation} \liminf_{kightarrow\infty}H(v_{n_k}) \ge\liminf_{kightarrow\infty}H(w_k)+ rac{(c_*-c)\delta}{2}>\liminf_{kightarrow\infty}H(w_k), \end{equation} which will lead to the desired contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: If the interaction term is $\le(c_*-c)\delta/2$ then (4.8) follows.

nodes.name: Bound the annulus term by three integrals (4.9)
nodes.statement:
To prove \eqref{est0}, we use the above properties of $u_k$ and $w_k$ to observe that  egin{multline} \left|\int_{R<|x|<R+a}\Big[|
abla v_{n_k}|^2-|
abla u_k|^2-|
abla w_k|^2 - rac{c}{|x|^2}\left(|v_{n_k}|^2-|u_k|^2-|w_k|^2ight)\Big]dxight| \ \le 5\int_{R<|x|<R+a}|
abla v_{n_k}|^2dx+4a^{-2}\int_{R<|x|<R+a}|v_{n_k}|^2dx + rac{3c}{R^2}\int_{R<|x|<R+a}|v_{n_k}|^2dx. \end{multline}
nodes.statement_short: Interaction term $\le 5\int|\nabla v|^2+4a^{-2}\int|v|^2+3cR^{-2}\int|v|^2$ over the annulus.

nodes.name: Potential term (4.10)
nodes.statement: First, by choosing $R>0$ sufficiently large, we will have \begin{equation} \frac{3c}{R^2}\int_{R<|x|<R+a}|v_{n_k}|^2dx \le \frac{3c}{R^2} \|v_{n_k}\|_{L^2}^2 \le \frac{(c_*-c)\delta}{4} \quad\text{for all} \ k\in\N. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Choose $R$ large so the $3c/R^2$ term is $\le(c_*-c)\delta/4$.

nodes.name: $L^2$ annulus term (4.11)
nodes.statement: The second term in the right-hand side of \eqref{est} is handled using Step 1 with $|y_k|\to\infty$: for any fixed $R,a>0$, we have that \begin{equation} \lim_{k\to\infty} \int_{R<|x|<R+a}|v_{n_k}|^2dx=0. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: By Step 1 with $|y_k|\to\infty$ the $L^2$ mass on any fixed annulus vanishes.

nodes.name: Claim: gradient annulus term (4.12)
nodes.statement:
As for the first term, we claim that we can choose $R>0$ as large as we want and $a>0$ such that, up to a subsequence,  egin{equation} 5\int_{R<|x|<R+a}|
abla v_{n_k}|^2dx\le  rac{(c_*-c)\delta}{4} \quad	ext{for all} \ k\in\N. \end{equation} Estimates \eqref{term3}--\eqref{term1} prove \eqref{est0}, and hence \eqref{e1}. If the above claim is not true, then using a diagonal argument we can construct a subsequence $\{v_{n_{k_l}}\}$, and a sequence of pairwise disjoint annuli \[ A_j=\{x\inn : R_j<|x|<R_j+a_j\} \quad	ext{with}\quad R_{j+1}>R_j+a_j, \] such that, for all $j\in\{1,\dots,l\}$, \[ \int_{A_j}|
abla v_{n_{k_l}}|^2dx\ge  ar \delta:=  rac{(c_*-c)\delta}{20}>0 \quad	ext{for all} \ n_{k_l}\in\N. \] But then \[ \intrn|
abla v_{n_{k_l}}|^2dx \ge \sum_{j\in\N}\int_{A_j}|
abla v_{n_{k_l}}|^2dx \ge \sum_{j=1}^l\int_{A_j}|
abla v_{n_{k_l}}|^2dx \ge l ar\delta, \] and it follows that \[ \lim_{l	o\infty}\intrn|
abla v_{n_{k_l}}|^2dx=+\infty. \] In view of \eqref{hardy2} this contradicts \eqref{a}, and completes the proof of \eqref{e1}.
nodes.statement_short: Choose $R,a$ with $5\int_{\rm annulus}|\nabla v_{n_k}|^2\le(c_*-c)\delta/4$; proved by a diagonal/pigeonhole argument.

nodes.name: State the claim (4.12) and its consequence
nodes.statement: As for the first term, we claim that we can choose $R>0$ as large as we want and $a>0$ such that, up to a subsequence, \begin{equation} 5\int_{R<|x|<R+a}|\nabla v_{n_k}|^2dx\le \frac{(c_*-c)\delta}{4} \quad\text{for all} \ k\in\N. \end{equation} Estimates \eqref{term3}--\eqref{term1} prove \eqref{est0}, and hence \eqref{e1}.
nodes.statement_short: With (4.10)–(4.12), (4.7) and hence (4.8) follow.

nodes.name: Suppose the claim fails: disjoint annuli
nodes.statement: If the above claim is not true, then using a diagonal argument we can construct a subsequence $\{v_{n_{k_l}}\}$, and a sequence of pairwise disjoint annuli \[ A_j=\{x\in\rn : R_j<|x|<R_j+a_j\} \quad\text{with}\quad R_{j+1}>R_j+a_j, \] such that, for all $j\in\{1,\dots,l\}$, \[ \int_{A_j}|\nabla v_{n_{k_l}}|^2dx\ge \bar \delta:= \frac{(c_*-c)\delta}{20}>0 \quad\text{for all} \ n_{k_l}\in\N. \]
nodes.statement_short: Diagonal argument yields disjoint annuli $A_j$ each carrying gradient mass $\ge\bar\delta$.

nodes.name: Gradient norm blows up
nodes.statement:
But then \[ \intrn|
abla v_{n_{k_l}}|^2dx \ge \sum_{j\in\N}\int_{A_j}|
abla v_{n_{k_l}}|^2dx \ge \sum_{j=1}^l\int_{A_j}|
abla v_{n_{k_l}}|^2dx \ge l ar\delta, \] and it follows that \[ \lim_{l	o\infty}\intrn|
abla v_{n_{k_l}}|^2dx=+\infty. \]
nodes.statement_short: Summing over $l$ annuli gives $\int|\nabla v_{n_{k_l}}|^2\ge l\bar\delta\to\infty$.

nodes.name: Contradiction with boundedness of $H$
nodes.statement: In view of \eqref{hardy2} this contradicts \eqref{a}, and completes the proof of \eqref{e1}.
nodes.statement_short: By (1.5) this contradicts (4.2), proving the claim and (4.8).

nodes.name: Combine (4.8) with the energy assumption
nodes.statement: We will now combine \eqref{e1} with the Gagliardo--Nirenberg inequality \eqref{GN} and the assumption on the energy in \eqref{a} to reach a contradiction. Using Step 1 with $|y_k|\to\infty$, we have that $u_k\to0$ in $L^{p+1}(\rn)$. Hence, by \eqref{a}, \begin{align*} \limsup_{k\rightarrow\infty}H(v_{n_k})\le\frac{2}{p+1}\liminf_{k\rightarrow\infty}\int_{\rn}|v_{n_k}|^{p+1}dx =\frac{2}{p+1}\liminf_{k\rightarrow\infty}\int_{\rn}|w_k|^{p+1}dx, \end{align*} and so, by \eqref{e1}, \begin{align} \liminf_{k\rightarrow\infty}H(w_k)<\frac{2}{p+1}\liminf_{k\rightarrow\infty}\int_{\rn}|w_k|^{p+1}dx. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Since $u_k\to0$ in $L^{p+1}$, (4.2) and (4.8) give $\liminf H(w_k)<\frac{2}{p+1}\liminf\int|w_k|^{p+1}$.

nodes.name: $w_k$ carries the full mass
nodes.statement: Using again Step 1 with $|y_k|\to\infty$, we also have that $u_k\to0$ in $L^2(\rn)$, which implies \[ M_\mathrm{gs}=\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}\|v_{n_k}\|_{L^2} =\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}\|w_k\|_{L^2}. \]
nodes.statement_short: $u_k\to0$ in $L^2$, so $\|w_k\|_{L^2}\to M_{\mathrm{gs}}$.

nodes.name: Gagliardo–Nirenberg contradiction; (4.5) proved
nodes.statement: Therefore, \eqref{GN} applied to $w_k$ yields \[ \frac{2}{p+1}\liminf_{k\rightarrow\infty}\int_{\rn}|w_k|^{p+1}dx \le\liminf_{k\rightarrow\infty}\left(\frac{\|w_k\|_{L^2}}{M_\mathrm{gs}}\right)^{\frac4N}H(w_k) = \liminf_{k\rightarrow\infty}H(w_k), \] which, together with \eqref{e4}, leads to the contradiction \[ \liminf_{k\rightarrow\infty}H(w_k)<\liminf_{k\rightarrow\infty}H(w_k). \] This shows that $\lim_{k\to\infty}\mathrm{I}_k=0$ and completes the proof of \eqref{zerolimit}.
nodes.statement_short: GN on $w_k$ gives $\liminf H(w_k)<\liminf H(w_k)$, so $\mathrm I_k\to0$ and (4.5) holds.

nodes.name: Lower bound on $\liminf E(v_{n_k})$
nodes.statement:
We now have  egin{align*} \liminf_{k	o\infty} E(v_{n_k}) &=\liminf_{k	o\infty}  rac12 \|
abla v_{n_k}\|_{L^2}^2 -\lim_{k	o\infty}  rac{1}{p+1} \| v_{n_k}\|_{L^{p+1}}^{p+1}\ &=\liminf_{k	o\infty}  rac12 \|
abla \wt{v}_{n_k}\|_{L^2}^2 -\lim_{k	o\infty}  rac{1}{p+1} \| \wt{v}_{n_k}\|_{L^{p+1}}^{p+1}\ &\ge  rac12 \|
abla v\|_{L^2}^2 -  rac{1}{p+1} \|v\|_{L^{p+1}}^{p+1}>E(v)\ge 0, \end{align*} where the last inequality follows from \eqref{posE} with $\|v\|_{L^2}=M_\mathrm{gs}$.
nodes.statement_short: With the potential term gone, $\liminf E(v_{n_k})\ge\frac12\|\nabla v\|^2-\frac1{p+1}\|v\|^{p+1}_{p+1}>E(v)\ge0$ by (1.8).

nodes.name: Conclude boundedness of $y_k$
nodes.statement: This contradicts \eqref{a} and shows that the sequence $\{y_k\}$ must indeed be bounded in $\rn$.
nodes.statement_short: Contradiction with $\limsup E(v_n)\le0$; the translations are bounded.

nodes.name: Step 3: conclusion
nodes.statement: {\em Step~3: Conclusion.} Suppose, without loss of generality, that $y_k\to y^*\in\rn$. Then \[ v_{n_k}\to v^*=v(\cdot+y^*) \quad \text{in} \quad L^q(\rn), \quad \forall q\in[2,2^*), \] and $v_{n_k}\wto v^*$ weakly in $H^1(\rn)$. Since the Hardy functional $H$ is weakly lower semi-continuous \cite{montefusco}, and $p+1\in(2,2^*)$, it now follows by \eqref{posE} that \[ \begin{split} 0\le E(v^*)=\frac{1}{2}H(v^*)-\frac{1}{p+1}\int_{\rn}|v^*|^{p+1}dx &\le \frac{1}{2}\limsup_{k\rightarrow\infty}H(v_{n_k})-\frac{1}{p+1}\int_{\rn}|v^*|^{p+1}dx\\ &\phantom{\le}=\limsup_{k\rightarrow\infty}E(v_{n_k})\le 0, \end{split} \] so in fact \begin{equation} E(v^*)=0 \quad\text{and}\quad H(v^*)=\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}H(v_{n_k}). \end{equation} Since $\|v^*\|_{L^2}=M_\mathrm{gs}$ and $E(v^*)=0$, Proposition \ref{charact.prop} yields $v^*=e^{i\gamma_0}Q_{\lambda_0}$ for some $\gamma_0\in\real$, $\lambda_0>0$, and some $Q\in \mathcal{G}$. Finally, by \eqref{convergence} and \eqref{hardy2}, we also have that $\|v_{n_k}\|_{H^1}\rightarrow \|v^*\|_{H^1}$. Hence $\{v_{n_k}\}$ converges strongly to $v^*$ in $H^1(\rn)$, which completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Pass to $y_k\to y^*$, get $E(v^*)=0$ with mass $M_{\mathrm{gs}}$, apply Proposition 3 and upgrade to strong $H^1$ convergence.

nodes.name: Pass to the limit of the translations
nodes.statement: {\em Step~3: Conclusion.} Suppose, without loss of generality, that $y_k\to y^*\in\rn$. Then \[ v_{n_k}\to v^*=v(\cdot+y^*) \quad \text{in} \quad L^q(\rn), \quad \forall q\in[2,2^*), \] and $v_{n_k}\wto v^*$ weakly in $H^1(\rn)$.
nodes.statement_short: WLOG $y_k\to y^*$; then $v_{n_k}\to v^*=v(\cdot+y^*)$ in $L^q$ and weakly in $H^1$.

nodes.name: $E(v^*)=0$ and $H(v^*)=\lim H(v_{n_k})$
nodes.statement: Since the Hardy functional $H$ is weakly lower semi-continuous \cite{montefusco}, and $p+1\in(2,2^*)$, it now follows by \eqref{posE} that \[ \begin{split} 0\le E(v^*)=\frac{1}{2}H(v^*)-\frac{1}{p+1}\int_{\rn}|v^*|^{p+1}dx &\le \frac{1}{2}\limsup_{k\rightarrow\infty}H(v_{n_k})-\frac{1}{p+1}\int_{\rn}|v^*|^{p+1}dx\\ &\phantom{\le}=\limsup_{k\rightarrow\infty}E(v_{n_k})\le 0, \end{split} \] so in fact \begin{equation} E(v^*)=0 \quad\text{and}\quad H(v^*)=\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}H(v_{n_k}). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Weak lower semicontinuity of $H$ and (1.8) squeeze $E(v^*)$ to $0$.

nodes.name: Apply Proposition 3
nodes.statement: Since $\|v^*\|_{L^2}=M_\mathrm{gs}$ and $E(v^*)=0$, Proposition \ref{charact.prop} yields $v^*=e^{i\gamma_0}Q_{\lambda_0}$ for some $\gamma_0\in\real$, $\lambda_0>0$, and some $Q\in \mathcal{G}$.
nodes.statement_short: $v^*=e^{i\gamma_0}Q_{\lambda_0}$ for a ground state $Q$.

nodes.name: Upgrade to strong $H^1$ convergence
nodes.statement: Finally, by \eqref{convergence} and \eqref{hardy2}, we also have that $\|v_{n_k}\|_{H^1}\rightarrow \|v^*\|_{H^1}$. Hence $\{v_{n_k}\}$ converges strongly to $v^*$ in $H^1(\rn)$, which completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Norm convergence plus weak convergence gives $v_{n_k}\to v^*$ in $H^1$.

nodes.name: Regularization
nodes.statement: By regularization we may assume that $u$ is smooth enough for the following calculation.
nodes.statement_short: WLOG $u$ is smooth enough for the computation.

nodes.name: Differentiate $\Gamma$ once
nodes.statement: Since $u$ satisfies (\ref{inls}), we find \[ \begin{split} \Gamma'(t)&=2\re\int|x|^2\bar{u}\partial_tu=2\re\int|x|^2\bar{u}i(\Delta u+\frac{c}{|x|^2}u+|u|^{p-1}u)\\ &=-2\im\int|x|^2(\bar{u}\Delta u+\frac{c}{|x|^2}|u|^2+|u|^{p+1})=-2\im\int|x|^2\bar{u}\Delta u. \end{split} \]
nodes.statement_short: $\Gamma'(t)=-2\,\mathrm{Im}\int|x|^2\bar u\Delta u$ using the equation.

nodes.name: First virial identity
nodes.statement:
Integrating by parts and using that $
abla |x|^2=2x$, we obtain \[ \Gamma'(t)=2\im\int
abla u( ar{u}
abla|x|^2+|x|^2
abla ar{u})=4\im\int ar{u}(
abla u\cdot x). \]
nodes.statement_short: Integration by parts gives $\Gamma'(t)=4\,\mathrm{Im}\int\bar u(\nabla u\cdot x)$.

nodes.name: Differentiate again
nodes.statement:
Using again integration by parts, we get \[  egin{split} \Gamma''(t)&=4\im\int\partial_t ar{u}(x\cdot
abla u)+ ar{u}(x\cdot
abla\partial_tu) =4\im\int\partial_tu[-x\cdot
abla ar{u}-
abla\cdot( ar{u}x)]\ &=4\im\int\partial_tu[-2x\cdot
abla ar{u}- ar{u}
abla\cdot x] =-8\im\int\partial_tu(x\cdot
abla ar{u})-4N\im\int\partial_tu ar{u}. \end{split} \]
nodes.statement_short: $\Gamma''(t)=-8\,\mathrm{Im}\int\partial_tu(x\cdot\nabla\bar u)-4N\,\mathrm{Im}\int\partial_tu\bar u$.

nodes.name: Compute the $-4N\,\mathrm{Im}\int\partial_tu\bar u$ term (4.17)
nodes.statement: We use (\ref{inls}) to compute the last two terms. We first find \begin{align} -4N\im\int\partial_tu\bar{u}&=-4N\re\int\bar{u}(\Delta u+\frac{c}{|x|^2}u+|u|^{p-1}u)\notag \\ &=4N\int{|\nabla u|^2}-4Nc\int\frac{|u|^2}{|x|^2}-4N\int|u|^{p+1}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Use the equation to express it through $\int|\nabla u|^2$, the potential and the $L^{p+1}$ term.

nodes.name: Split the remaining term into $A+B+C$
nodes.statement:
Similarly, \[  egin{split} -8\im\int\partial_tu(x\cdot 
abla  ar{u})&= -8e\int(x\cdot
abla ar{u})(\Delta u+ rac{c}{|x|^2}u+|u|^{p-1}u) \ &=-8e\int\Delta u(x\cdot
abla ar{u})-8c\int|x|^{-2}x\cdote(u
abla ar{u}) -8\int x\cdot|u|^{p-1}e(u
abla ar{u}) \ &\equiv A+B+C. \end{split} \]
nodes.statement_short: Express $-8\,\mathrm{Im}\int\partial_tu(x\cdot\nabla\bar u)$ as three integrals $A$, $B$, $C$.

nodes.name: Compute $A$ (4.18)
nodes.statement:
Since $\partial_{x_k}(|\partial_{x_j}u|^2) = 2e(\partial_{x_j}u\partial_{x_j}\partial_{x_k} ar u)$ for $1\le j,k\le N$, we find  egin{align} A &= -8\sum_{j,k} e\int \partial_{x_j}^2u\, x_k\partial_{x_k} ar u = 8\sum_{j,k} e\int \partial_{x_j}u (\delta_{j,k}\partial_{x_k} ar u + x_k\partial_{x_j}\partial_{x_k} ar u) 
otag \ &= 8\sum_j \int |\partial_{x_j}u|^2 +4\sum_{j,k} \int x_k\partial_{x_k}(|\partial_{x_j}u|^2) 
otag \ &= 8\sum_j \int |\partial_{x_j}u|^2 -4\sum_{j,k} \int |\partial_{x_j}u|^2 = (8-4N)\int |
abla u|^2, \end{align} where $\delta_{j,k}=1$ for $j=k$ and $0$ otherwise.
nodes.statement_short: Integration by parts: $A=(8-4N)\int|\nabla u|^2$.

nodes.name: Compute $C$ (4.19)
Compute $B$ (4.20)
nodes.statement_short: $B=4c\int|u|^2(N-2)|x|^{-2}$ by integration by parts.

nodes.name: Assemble the second virial identity
nodes.statement: Finally, putting together (\ref{viriala}), (\ref{virialpart3}), (\ref{virialc}) and (\ref{viriald}), we obtain \[ \begin{split} \Gamma''(t)&=8\int|\nabla u|^2-8c\int\frac{|u|^2}{|x|^2}+\frac{4}{p+1}(N-Np)\int|u|^{p+1} \\ &=16E(u)+\frac{4}{p+1}(N-Np+4)\int|u|^{p+1}, \end{split} \] which concludes the proof.

nodes.name: Setting
nodes.statement: Let $u$ be a solution of \eqref{inls} such that $\|u\|_{L^2}=M_\mathrm{gs}$ and $\lim_{t\uparrow T} H(u) =+\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix a minimal mass solution blowing up at $T$.

nodes.name: Step 1: rescaled profiles converge to a ground state
nodes.statement: {\em Step~1.} Let $\{t_n\}_{n\in\nat} \subset \real$ be a sequence of times such that $t_n\uparrow T$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$. We set \[ u_n=u(t_n), \quad \lambda_n^2=H(u_n), \quad v_n(x)=\lambda_n^{-N/2}u_n(\lambda_n^{-1}x). \] We note that $\lambda_n\rightarrow\infty$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$, and $\|v_n\|_{L^2}=\|u_n\|_{L^2}=\|u_0\|_{L^2}=M_\mathrm{gs}$ by the $L^2$ scaling. Furthermore, \[ \begin{split} H(v_n)=\lambda_n^{-2}H(u_n)=1. \end{split} \] On the other hand, by conservation of the energy, \[ \begin{split} E(v_n)&=\frac12\lambda_n^{-2}H(u_n)-\frac{1}{p+1}\lambda_n^{-2}\int_{\rn} |u_n(y)|^{p+1}dy\\ &=\lambda_n^{-2} E(u_n)=\lambda_n^{-2}E(u_0)\to 0 \quad \text{as} \ n\to\infty. \end{split} \] Hence, by Proposition \ref{compact.prop}, there exist $Q\in\mathcal{G}$, $\gamma_0\in\real$ and $\lambda_0>0$ such that, up to a subsequence, \begin{equation} \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \|v_n-e^{i\gamma_0}Q_{\lambda_0}\|_{H^1}=0, \end{equation} where $Q_{\lambda_0}(x)=\lambda_0^{N/2}Q(\lambda_0 x)$.
nodes.statement_short: Rescale $u(t_n)$ by $\lambda_n^2=H(u_n)$; Proposition 4 gives $v_n\to e^{i\gamma_0}Q_{\lambda_0}$ in $H^1$.

nodes.name: Define the rescaled sequence $v_n$
nodes.statement: {\em Step~1.} Let $\{t_n\}_{n\in\nat} \subset \real$ be a sequence of times such that $t_n\uparrow T$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$. We set \[ u_n=u(t_n), \quad \lambda_n^2=H(u_n), \quad v_n(x)=\lambda_n^{-N/2}u_n(\lambda_n^{-1}x). \]
nodes.statement_short: Take $t_n\uparrow T$, $u_n=u(t_n)$, $\lambda_n^2=H(u_n)$, $v_n=\lambda_n^{-N/2}u_n(\lambda_n^{-1}\cdot)$.

nodes.name: Mass and $H$ of $v_n$
nodes.statement: We note that $\lambda_n\rightarrow\infty$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$, and $\|v_n\|_{L^2}=\|u_n\|_{L^2}=\|u_0\|_{L^2}=M_\mathrm{gs}$ by the $L^2$ scaling. Furthermore, \[ \begin{split} H(v_n)=\lambda_n^{-2}H(u_n)=1. \end{split} \]
nodes.statement_short: $\|v_n\|_{L^2}=M_{\mathrm{gs}}$ and $H(v_n)=1$.

nodes.name: Energy of $v_n$ tends to $0$
nodes.statement: On the other hand, by conservation of the energy, \[ \begin{split} E(v_n)&=\frac12\lambda_n^{-2}H(u_n)-\frac{1}{p+1}\lambda_n^{-2}\int_{\rn} |u_n(y)|^{p+1}dy\\ &=\lambda_n^{-2} E(u_n)=\lambda_n^{-2}E(u_0)\to 0 \quad \text{as} \ n\to\infty. \end{split} \]
nodes.statement_short: $E(v_n)=\lambda_n^{-2}E(u_0)\to0$.

nodes.name: Apply Proposition 4
nodes.statement: Hence, by Proposition \ref{compact.prop}, there exist $Q\in\mathcal{G}$, $\gamma_0\in\real$ and $\lambda_0>0$ such that, up to a subsequence, \begin{equation} \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \|v_n-e^{i\gamma_0}Q_{\lambda_0}\|_{H^1}=0, \end{equation} where $Q_{\lambda_0}(x)=\lambda_0^{N/2}Q(\lambda_0 x)$.
nodes.statement_short: Up to a subsequence $v_n\to e^{i\gamma_0}Q_{\lambda_0}$ in $H^1$ (4.23).

nodes.name: Step 2: mass concentration at the origin
nodes.statement: {\em Step~2.} We now prove that $u_n$ concentrates all of its mass at $x=0$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$. We show that, in the sense of distributions, \[ |u_n|^2\rightarrow M_\mathrm{gs}^2\delta_0. \] Indeed, for any $\varphi\in C^\infty_0(\rn)$, using the change of variables $y=\lambda_n^{-1}x$ we find that \[ \begin{split} \int_{\rn}|u_n(y)|^2\varphi(y)dy &=\int_{\rn}|u_n(\lambda_n^{-1}x)|^2\varphi(\lambda^{-1}_nx)\lambda_n^{-N}dx =\int_{\rn}|v_n(x)|^2\varphi(\lambda_n^{-1}x)dx\\ &=\int_{\rn}(|v_n(x)|^2-|Q(x)|^2)\varphi(\lambda_n^{-1}x)dx+\int_{\rn} |Q(x)|^2\varphi(0)dx\\ &\phantom{\le} \ +\int_{\rn}|Q(x)|^2(\varphi(\lambda_n^{-1}x)-\varphi(0))dx. \end{split} \] Thus, we obtain \[ \begin{split} \Big|\int_{\rn}|u_n(y)|^2\varphi(y)dy -M_\mathrm{gs}^2\varphi(0)\Big| &\le \|\varphi\|_{L^\infty}\int_{\rn}||v_n(x)|^2-|Q(x)|^2|dx\\ &\phantom{\le} \ +\int_{\rn}|Q(x)|^2|\varphi(\lambda_n^{-1}x)-\varphi(0)|dx. \end{split} \] We conclude this step by noticing that $|v_n|^2$ converges strongly to $|Q|^2$ in $L^1(\rn)$ from (\ref{b}), so the first integral vanishes as $n\rightarrow\infty$. Since $\lambda_n\rightarrow\infty$ the second integral also converges to zero by the dominated convergence theorem. Hence, we obtain \begin{equation} \int_{\rn}|u_n(y)|^2\varphi(y)dy\rightarrow M_\mathrm{gs}^2\varphi(0). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $|u_n|^2\to M_{\mathrm{gs}}^2\delta_0$ in the sense of distributions.

nodes.name: State the concentration claim
nodes.statement: {\em Step~2.} We now prove that $u_n$ concentrates all of its mass at $x=0$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$. We show that, in the sense of distributions, \[ |u_n|^2\rightarrow M_\mathrm{gs}^2\delta_0. \]
nodes.statement_short: Show $|u_n|^2\to M_{\mathrm{gs}}^2\delta_0$ in $\mathcal D'$.

nodes.name: Change of variables
nodes.statement: Indeed, for any $\varphi\in C^\infty_0(\rn)$, using the change of variables $y=\lambda_n^{-1}x$ we find that \[ \begin{split} \int_{\rn}|u_n(y)|^2\varphi(y)dy &=\int_{\rn}|u_n(\lambda_n^{-1}x)|^2\varphi(\lambda^{-1}_nx)\lambda_n^{-N}dx =\int_{\rn}|v_n(x)|^2\varphi(\lambda_n^{-1}x)dx\\ &=\int_{\rn}(|v_n(x)|^2-|Q(x)|^2)\varphi(\lambda_n^{-1}x)dx+\int_{\rn} |Q(x)|^2\varphi(0)dx\\ &\phantom{\le} \ +\int_{\rn}|Q(x)|^2(\varphi(\lambda_n^{-1}x)-\varphi(0))dx. \end{split} \]
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite $\int|u_n|^2\varphi$ via $v_n$ and split off $M_{\mathrm{gs}}^2\varphi(0)$.

nodes.name: Bound the error
nodes.statement: Thus, we obtain \[ \begin{split} \Big|\int_{\rn}|u_n(y)|^2\varphi(y)dy -M_\mathrm{gs}^2\varphi(0)\Big| &\le \|\varphi\|_{L^\infty}\int_{\rn}||v_n(x)|^2-|Q(x)|^2|dx\\ &\phantom{\le} \ +\int_{\rn}|Q(x)|^2|\varphi(\lambda_n^{-1}x)-\varphi(0)|dx. \end{split} \]
nodes.statement_short: Error $\le\|\varphi\|_\infty\int||v_n|^2-|Q|^2|+\int|Q|^2|\varphi(\lambda_n^{-1}x)-\varphi(0)|$.

nodes.name: Both error terms vanish
nodes.statement: We conclude this step by noticing that $|v_n|^2$ converges strongly to $|Q|^2$ in $L^1(\rn)$ from (\ref{b}), so the first integral vanishes as $n\rightarrow\infty$. Since $\lambda_n\rightarrow\infty$ the second integral also converges to zero by the dominated convergence theorem. Hence, we obtain \begin{equation} \int_{\rn}|u_n(y)|^2\varphi(y)dy\rightarrow M_\mathrm{gs}^2\varphi(0). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Strong $L^1$ convergence from (4.23) and dominated convergence give (4.24).

nodes.name: Step 3: $u(t)\in\Sigma$ and the variance identity
nodes.statement:
{\em Step~3.} We now show that $u(t)\in\Sigma$ for all $t\in[0,T)$. Let $\phi\in C^\infty_0(n)$ be a radial and non-negative function such that $\phi(x)=|x|^2$ for $|x|\le 1$. It is easy to see that there exists a constant $C>0$ such that \[ |
abla \phi (x) |^2\le C\phi(x) \] for all $x\inn$. Indeed, since $\phi$ is radially symmetric we may choose $f\in C(eal,eal_+) $, such that $\phi(|x|)=f(|x|)$. By Taylor's formula, for all $r\ineal$ and $h\ineal$ there exists $y\in[r,r+h]$, such that \[ 0\le f(r+h)=f(r)+f'(r)h+ rac{f''(y)}{2}h^2\le f(r)+f'(r)h+C'h^2, \] where $C'=1+\max_{r\ineal} rac{|f'(r)|}{2}>0$. Since the right-hand side is a positive quadratic polynomial, we must have that $|f'(r)|^2-4C'f(r)\le 0$, thus $|f'(r)|^2\le Cf(r)$, where $C=4C'>0$. For all $R>0$, we define $\phi_R(x)=R^2\phi(x/R)$, and for all $t\in[0,T)$, \[ \Gamma_R(t)=\int_{n}\phi_R(x)|u(t,x)|^2dx. \] A direct calculation, similar to the proof of Lemma~ef{virial.lemma}, yields that \[ \Gamma_R'(t)=2	ext{Re}\int\phi_R ar{u}\partial_tu =-2	ext{Im}\int\phi_R ar{u}(\Delta u+ rac{c}{|x|^2}u+|u|^{p-1}u) =2\int
abla\phi_R\cdot	ext{Im}( ar{u}
abla u). \] Since $\|u\|_{L^2}=\|Q\|_{L^2}$, we can apply Lemma ef{banica.lem} and the inequality $|
abla\phi_R|^2\le C\phi_R$, to get \[ |\Gamma'_R(t)|\le 2\sqrt{2E(u)}\Big(\int|
abla\phi_R|^2|u|^2\Big)^{1/2} \le C\sqrt{E(u_0)}\sqrt{\Gamma_R(t)}. \] By integrating between a fixed $t\in[0,T)$ and $t_n$, we obtain, \[ |\sqrt{\Gamma_R(t)}-\sqrt{\Gamma_R(t_n)}|\le C|t-t_n|. \] Applying (ef{c}) in Step 2, we get \[ \Gamma_R(t_n)=\int_{n} |u_n(x)|^2\phi_R(x)dxightarrow M_\mathrm{gs}^2\phi_R(0)=0. \] Thus, letting $n	o\infty$ in the last inequality, we obtain, for all $t\in [0,T)$ and all $R>0$, \[ \Gamma_R(t) \le C(T-t)^2. \] Since the right-hand side of the last expression is independent of $R$, letting $R	o\infty$ yields, for all $t\in [0,T)$, \[ u(t)\in\Sigma \quad	ext{and}\quad 0\le \Gamma(t) \le C(T-t)^2. \] From this estimate, we can extend by continuity $\Gamma(t)$ at $t=T$ by setting $\Gamma(T)=0$, from which we also obtain $\Gamma'(T)=0$. Moreover, since $u(t)\in\Sigma$ and $u$ is a solution of~\eqref{inls}, we may apply Lemma~ef{virial.lemma}, and by (ef{virialthree}) we obtain $\Gamma''(t)=16E(u_0)$, which finally gives, for all $t\in [0,T)$, \[ \Gamma(t) = 8E(u_0)(T-t)^2. \] Letting $t=0$, we find, using identity (ef{virialone}) \[ \Gamma(0)=\int |x|^2|u_0|^2= 8E(u_0)T^2 \quad 	ext{and}\quad \Gamma'(0)= 4\int x\cdot\im(\overline{u_0}
abla u_0) = -16E(u_0)T. \]
nodes.statement_short: Localized virial with Banica's inequality shows $\Gamma_R(t)\le C(T-t)^2$, so $u(t)\in\Sigma$ and $\Gamma(t)=8E(u_0)(T-t)^2$.

nodes.name: Choose the localizing weight $\phi$
nodes.statement: {\em Step~3.} We now show that $u(t)\in\Sigma$ for all $t\in[0,T)$. Let $\phi\in C^\infty_0(\rn)$ be a radial and non-negative function such that $\phi(x)=|x|^2$ for $|x|\le 1$. It is easy to see that there exists a constant $C>0$ such that \[ |\nabla \phi (x) |^2\le C\phi(x) \] for all $x\in\rn$.
nodes.statement_short: Radial nonnegative $\phi$ with $\phi=|x|^2$ near $0$ and $|\nabla\phi|^2\le C\phi$.

nodes.name: Justify $|\nabla\phi|^2\le C\phi$
nodes.statement: Indeed, since $\phi$ is radially symmetric we may choose $f\in C(\real,\real_+) $, such that $\phi(|x|)=f(|x|)$. By Taylor's formula, for all $r\in\real$ and $h\in\real$ there exists $y\in[r,r+h]$, such that \[ 0\le f(r+h)=f(r)+f'(r)h+\frac{f''(y)}{2}h^2\le f(r)+f'(r)h+C'h^2, \] where $C'=1+\max_{r\in\real}\frac{|f'(r)|}{2}>0$. Since the right-hand side is a positive quadratic polynomial, we must have that $|f'(r)|^2-4C'f(r)\le 0$, thus $|f'(r)|^2\le Cf(r)$, where $C=4C'>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Taylor's formula and positivity of a quadratic polynomial give $|f'|^2\le Cf$.

nodes.name: Localized variance $\Gamma_R$ and its derivative
nodes.statement: For all $R>0$, we define $\phi_R(x)=R^2\phi(x/R)$, and for all $t\in[0,T)$, \[ \Gamma_R(t)=\int_{\rn}\phi_R(x)|u(t,x)|^2dx. \] A direct calculation, similar to the proof of Lemma~\ref{virial.lemma}, yields that \[ \Gamma_R'(t)=2\text{Re}\int\phi_R\bar{u}\partial_tu =-2\text{Im}\int\phi_R\bar{u}(\Delta u+\frac{c}{|x|^2}u+|u|^{p-1}u) =2\int\nabla\phi_R\cdot\text{Im}(\bar{u}\nabla u). \]
nodes.statement_short: Define $\Gamma_R(t)=\int\phi_R|u|^2$; then $\Gamma_R'=2\int\nabla\phi_R\cdot\mathrm{Im}(\bar u\nabla u)$.

nodes.name: Apply Banica's inequality
nodes.statement: Since $\|u\|_{L^2}=\|Q\|_{L^2}$, we can apply Lemma \ref{banica.lem} and the inequality $|\nabla\phi_R|^2\le C\phi_R$, to get \[ |\Gamma'_R(t)|\le 2\sqrt{2E(u)}\Big(\int|\nabla\phi_R|^2|u|^2\Big)^{1/2} \le C\sqrt{E(u_0)}\sqrt{\Gamma_R(t)}. \]
nodes.statement_short: $|\Gamma_R'(t)|\le C\sqrt{E(u_0)}\sqrt{\Gamma_R(t)}$.

nodes.name: Integrate the differential inequality
nodes.statement: By integrating between a fixed $t\in[0,T)$ and $t_n$, we obtain, \[ |\sqrt{\Gamma_R(t)}-\sqrt{\Gamma_R(t_n)}|\le C|t-t_n|. \]
nodes.statement_short: $|\sqrt{\Gamma_R(t)}-\sqrt{\Gamma_R(t_n)}|\le C|t-t_n|$.

nodes.name: Let $n\to\infty$ using concentration
nodes.statement: Applying (\ref{c}) in Step 2, we get \[ \Gamma_R(t_n)=\int_{\rn} |u_n(x)|^2\phi_R(x)dx\rightarrow M_\mathrm{gs}^2\phi_R(0)=0. \] Thus, letting $n\to\infty$ in the last inequality, we obtain, for all $t\in [0,T)$ and all $R>0$, \[ \Gamma_R(t) \le C(T-t)^2. \]
nodes.statement_short: $\Gamma_R(t_n)\to0$ by (4.24), hence $\Gamma_R(t)\le C(T-t)^2$.

nodes.name: Let $R\to\infty$: $u(t)\in\Sigma$
nodes.statement: Since the right-hand side of the last expression is independent of $R$, letting $R\to\infty$ yields, for all $t\in [0,T)$, \[ u(t)\in\Sigma \quad\text{and}\quad 0\le \Gamma(t) \le C(T-t)^2. \] From this estimate, we can extend by continuity $\Gamma(t)$ at $t=T$ by setting $\Gamma(T)=0$, from which we also obtain $\Gamma'(T)=0$.
nodes.statement_short: $u(t)\in\Sigma$, $0\le\Gamma(t)\le C(T-t)^2$, and $\Gamma(T)=\Gamma'(T)=0$ by continuity.

nodes.name: Virial identities give $\Gamma(t)=8E(u_0)(T-t)^2$
nodes.statement: Moreover, since $u(t)\in\Sigma$ and $u$ is a solution of~\eqref{inls}, we may apply Lemma~\ref{virial.lemma}, and by (\ref{virialthree}) we obtain $\Gamma''(t)=16E(u_0)$, which finally gives, for all $t\in [0,T)$, \[ \Gamma(t) = 8E(u_0)(T-t)^2. \] Letting $t=0$, we find, using identity (\ref{virialone}) \[ \Gamma(0)=\int |x|^2|u_0|^2= 8E(u_0)T^2 \quad \text{and}\quad \Gamma'(0)= 4\int x\cdot\im(\overline{u_0}\nabla u_0) = -16E(u_0)T. \]
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 3 and (4.21) yield $\Gamma''=16E(u_0)$, hence $\Gamma(0)=8E(u_0)T^2$ and $\Gamma'(0)=-16E(u_0)T$.

nodes.name: Step 4: identify $u_0$ and conclude
nodes.statement: {\em Step 4.} We apply identity \eqref{valeria} with $u_0$, $s=\frac{1}{2T}$, and $\theta(x)=\frac{|x|^2}{2}$ to get \[ \begin{split} E(u_0e^{i\frac{|x|^2}{4T}})&=E(u_0)+\frac{1}{2T}\int x\cdot\text{Im}(\bar{u_0}\nabla u_0) +\frac{1}{8T^2}\int|x|^2|u_0|^2\\ &=E(u_0)+\frac{1}{2T}(-4E(u_0))+\frac{1}{8T^2}(8E(u_0)T^2)=0. \end{split} \] Note that this calculation justifies, {\em a posteriori}, the application of~\eqref{valeria} with $\theta(x)=\frac{|x|^2}{2}\not\in C_0^{\infty}(\rn)$. Since $\|u_0e^{i\frac{|x|^2}{4T}}\|_{L^2}=M_\mathrm{gs}$ and $E(u_0e^{i\frac{|x|^2}{4T}})=0$, we can deduce from Proposition \ref{charact.prop} that there exist $\lambda_1>0$, $\gamma_1\in\real$, and $\wt{Q}\in\mathcal{G}$ such that \[ u_0(x)=e^{i\gamma_1}e^{-i\frac{|x|^2}{4T}}\lambda_1^{N/2}\wt{Q}(\lambda_1x). \] Finally, we use the pseudo-conformal transformation. We define $\tilde\lambda_0=\lambda_1T>0$ and $\tilde\gamma_0=\gamma_1-\lambda_1^2T\in\real$, and write $u_0$ as \[ u_0(x)=e^{i\tilde\gamma_0}e^{i\frac{\tilde\lambda^2_0}{T}} e^{-i\frac{|x|^2}{4T}}\Big(\frac{\tilde\lambda_0}{T}\Big)^{N/2}\wt{Q}\Big(\frac{\tilde\lambda_0x}{T}\Big). \] Thus, $u_0=S_{\wt{Q},T,\tilde\lambda_0,\tilde\gamma_0}(0)$, where $S_{\wt{Q},T,\tilde\lambda_0,\tilde\gamma_0}$ is defined by (\ref{S2.def}). By invoking uniqueness of the solution of (\ref{inls}), we find that $u(t)=S_{\wt{Q},T,\tilde\lambda_0,\tilde\gamma_0}(t)$ for all $t\in[0,T)$, which concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: The modulated datum $u_0e^{i|x|^2/4T}$ has zero energy, so Proposition 3 and the pseudo-conformal transform identify $u_0=S_{\tilde Q,T,\tilde\lambda_0,\tilde\gamma_0}(0)$; uniqueness finishes.

nodes.name: Zero energy of the modulated datum
nodes.statement: {\em Step 4.} We apply identity \eqref{valeria} with $u_0$, $s=\frac{1}{2T}$, and $\theta(x)=\frac{|x|^2}{2}$ to get \[ \begin{split} E(u_0e^{i\frac{|x|^2}{4T}})&=E(u_0)+\frac{1}{2T}\int x\cdot\text{Im}(\bar{u_0}\nabla u_0) +\frac{1}{8T^2}\int|x|^2|u_0|^2\\ &=E(u_0)+\frac{1}{2T}(-4E(u_0))+\frac{1}{8T^2}(8E(u_0)T^2)=0. \end{split} \] Note that this calculation justifies, {\em a posteriori}, the application of~\eqref{valeria} with $\theta(x)=\frac{|x|^2}{2}\not\in C_0^{\infty}(\rn)$.

nodes.name: Apply Proposition 3
nodes.statement: Since $\|u_0e^{i\frac{|x|^2}{4T}}\|_{L^2}=M_\mathrm{gs}$ and $E(u_0e^{i\frac{|x|^2}{4T}})=0$, we can deduce from Proposition \ref{charact.prop} that there exist $\lambda_1>0$, $\gamma_1\in\real$, and $\wt{Q}\in\mathcal{G}$ such that \[ u_0(x)=e^{i\gamma_1}e^{-i\frac{|x|^2}{4T}}\lambda_1^{N/2}\wt{Q}(\lambda_1x). \]
nodes.statement_short: $u_0=e^{i\gamma_1}e^{-i|x|^2/4T}\lambda_1^{N/2}\tilde Q(\lambda_1x)$.

nodes.name: Rewrite $u_0$ in the form $S(0)$
nodes.statement: Finally, we use the pseudo-conformal transformation. We define $\tilde\lambda_0=\lambda_1T>0$ and $\tilde\gamma_0=\gamma_1-\lambda_1^2T\in\real$, and write $u_0$ as \[ u_0(x)=e^{i\tilde\gamma_0}e^{i\frac{\tilde\lambda^2_0}{T}} e^{-i\frac{|x|^2}{4T}}\Big(\frac{\tilde\lambda_0}{T}\Big)^{N/2}\wt{Q}\Big(\frac{\tilde\lambda_0x}{T}\Big). \]
nodes.statement_short: Set $\tilde\lambda_0=\lambda_1T$, $\tilde\gamma_0=\gamma_1-\lambda_1^2T$.

nodes.name: Conclude by uniqueness
nodes.statement: Thus, $u_0=S_{\wt{Q},T,\tilde\lambda_0,\tilde\gamma_0}(0)$, where $S_{\wt{Q},T,\tilde\lambda_0,\tilde\gamma_0}$ is defined by (\ref{S2.def}). By invoking uniqueness of the solution of (\ref{inls}), we find that $u(t)=S_{\wt{Q},T,\tilde\lambda_0,\tilde\gamma_0}(t)$ for all $t\in[0,T)$, which concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: $u_0=S(0)$, so by uniqueness $u(t)=S_{\tilde Q,T,\tilde\lambda_0,\tilde\gamma_0}(t)$.
